newsitem.title: UK: Focus - Barclays merges fund management units.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Barclays merges fund management units.

text.p: Britain's Barclays Plc said on Tuesday it was merging its two fund management businesses into a San Francisco-headquartered firm called Barclays Global Investors.

The integration of BZW Barclays Global Investors and BZW Investment Management under one management and one name will unify the investment styles of the two, Lindsay Tomlinson, joint chief executive of the merged group told Reuters.

Fred Grauer, formerly chairman of BZW Barclays Global Investors, has been made head of Barclays Global Investors, which will have some 230 billion pounds ($364 billion) in funds under management, the group said in a statement.

Grauer said the integration would make it more effective in providing reliable investment performance, add the convenience of dealing with a single global firm, and provide benefits from the increased scale of operations.

Tomlinson said there would be some redundancies in the "active equity area of the business", adding that 11 fund management staff had left the company overnight. He said the U.S. still accounted for the bulk of the firm's funds under management.

Barclays Global Investors will be part of the Barclays Plc's Asset Management Group, which is chaired by John Varley. It became Barclays' second fund management business last year, when the bank bought Wells Fargo Nikko Investment Advisers for $440 million and rechristened it BZW Barclays Global Investors.

The integration is part of Barclays' efforts to grab a larger share of the world's growing pension management business, a central plank of which is the use of sophisticated quantitative management techniques.
Barclays Global Investors uses quantitative techniques to manage funds, controlling risks and costs through application of technology and strict methodology.
It estimates that the quantitative method, which was developed in the United States in the 1970s and 1980s, costs pension funds around one-tenth of the average cost for an actively managed fund.
The division said earlier this year that around 15 percent of the U.S. stockmarket is now owned by funds using quantitative management and that figure could rise to 50 percent.
It expects to be managing $500 billion by the end of the decade and says that these economies of scale will benefit its clients.
